Dana, yes—you can do this yourself. Allow 2–3 hours with a helper rather than counting on twenty minutes. $465 isn’t a ripoff for doing both systems properly, but learning the job is worthwhile.

Hector, one correction before Dana buys supplies: don’t use green automotive antifreeze for this. Ethylene glycol is toxic, and automotive antifreeze isn’t rated for this raw-water winterizing job. Use pink propylene glycol RV/marine antifreeze specifically labeled for the engine’s raw-water system and potable-water plumbing. Neither kind belongs in the river.

Your 3GM30F has two separate cooling circuits. The closed freshwater circuit carries coolant through the engine and heat exchanger. Check its strength with a hydrometer suitable for that coolant; a proper 50/50 mix should protect to about -20°F. If it’s weak or due for replacement, address that separately. The raw-water circuit brings seawater through the strainer, pump and heat exchanger, then sends it out through the exhaust. That’s the side people miss, and trapped water can freeze and crack things.

Here’s the order I’d follow:

1. Get supplies and read the Yanmar and antifreeze manufacturers’ winterizing procedures first. Figure roughly two gallons of pink for the engine and another two or three for the domestic water system, but those are shopping estimates, not completion marks. Buy enough to finish the procedures and verify protection. It’s roughly $6 a gallon at West Marine or Walmart; check the label, not just the color. Have oil, filter, fuel stabilizer and a spare raw-water impeller aboard.

2. Before starting, arrange to capture everything coming out of the exhaust—ordinary cooling water as well as the winterizing mixture—for appropriate disposal ashore. Have your helper watch both exhaust flow and collection throughout every engine run. Don’t obstruct the exhaust or let collection back up.

3. Warm the engine with its normal cooling-water supply, then stop it and change the oil and filter while warm. Top up the fuel tank without overfilling, add the correct dose of diesel stabilizer, and run about ten minutes to circulate it. Check for oil leaks and recheck the oil level afterward.

4. Stop the engine before changing the raw-water supply. Close the intake seacock, then arrange the strainer/intake feed to draw antifreeze as specified in the winterizing procedure. Run at idle, keeping the pump supplied and wet the whole time. Your helper watches the exhaust and collection while you watch the supply. Don’t let the jug empty and run the impeller dry.

Follow the engine and antifreeze instructions through completion, and test the discharged mixture with the appropriate tester for the required winter protection. Seeing pink at the exhaust is not proof: residual water dilutes it. Shut down when complete, restore and secure the plumbing, and leave the seacock closed. Tag the engine controls so nobody starts it that way.

You can remove and inspect the old impeller afterward if you want; replace it if suspect, and keep a spare aboard regardless.

5. For the domestic water, switch off the water-heater breaker before draining anything. Leave it off until the heater is refilled in spring. Drain the freshwater tank and the heater, then use the heater bypass behind the companionway steps on your Catalina. Otherwise you’ll waste six gallons of pink filling the heater. Follow the water-system winterizing procedure, treating every hot and cold outlet and any other connected fixtures. Collect that discharge too, and verify the required protection rather than stopping at the first pink trickle.

The Christmas freeze a few years back cracked exhaust elbows or strainers on three boats on C dock. All three had skipped or rushed the raw-water side. That’s where a careful afternoon beats a hurried jug-through-the-engine job.

I’m happy to come down Saturday morning if you’d like a second set of hands.
